strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and important bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction: the quadratic global attention cost in VGGT-style models. The runtime motivation is well supported, especially for large frame counts where global attention dominates inference.

The proposed retrofit is practically attractive: it is training-free for the main method, preserves the pretrained VGGT/pi3 backbones, treats special tokens separately, and uses block-sparse kernels in a way that can plausibly be integrated into existing inference stacks.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this problem setting, covering relative pose, pointmap estimation, and scene-level pose estimation across Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D, and Tanks & Temples.

The results support a useful accuracy-efficiency tradeoff. Low-to-moderate sparsity settings often preserve accuracy very closely, and large-sequence Tanks & Temples timings show substantial end-to-end speedups, e.g. full-length VGGT from 35s to 14.4s at S50 and pi3 from 27.9s to 11.3s at S50.

The attention analysis and layer-drop ablations give a plausible mechanistic story: middle global-attention layers appear most important, and patch-patch attention is much more selective than interactions involving special tokens. The special-token ablation also supports a specific design choice.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate. The core mechanism is largely an adaptation/simplification of existing block-sparse attention ideas, especially SpargeAttention/SeerAttention-style mask prediction, to VGGT and pi3. The paper would be stronger if it more directly isolated what is technically new beyond applying known sparse-attention machinery to this architecture.

The main comparison lacks a direct sparse-attention baseline under the same conditions. Since the method is explicitly motivated by SpargeAttention, comparisons to full SpargeAttention variants, fixed local/global sparse masks, random/block top-k masks, or simpler layer skipping would be important to establish that the proposed adaptive mask is the right design.

The speedup claims need more careful framing. Gains are compelling for long sequences, but for 25-frame inputs the method is sometimes slower than dense attention, and even at 50 frames the gains vary. The abstract-level 'up to 4x' claim is true only in large-input regimes and should not be read as a general inference speedup.

The definition and reporting of sparsity are confusing. The text says sparsity is the ratio of computed entries to total entries, but elsewhere a sparsity ratio of 0.75 implies a 4x theoretical speedup, which corresponds to skipping 75% of entries. Tables and figures would be easier to interpret with consistent terminology such as kept-block ratio versus skipped-block ratio.

The evaluation appears to sweep Top-k/CDF settings and report many test results, but the protocol for choosing operating points is not clearly specified. Without a validation selection procedure, the accuracy-speed tradeoff may be partially test-tuned.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. Important implementation details such as exact block sizes for the main method, kernel configuration, memory measurements, batching policy, warmup/timing protocol, and whether code will be released are either absent or scattered. These details matter because sparse attention speedups are highly hardware- and implementation-dependent.

The paper mostly evaluates downstream aggregate metrics and selected qualitative examples. It does not deeply analyze failure cases, per-scene robustness, sensitivity to viewpoint overlap/texture/repeated structure at high sparsity, or uncertainty introduced by approximate attention, even though high sparsity causes substantial pose degradation in several settings.

strengths: The paper targets a real bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view geometry models: global attention becomes dominant as the number of frames grows. The motivation is clear and practically relevant.

The proposed modification is simple and appealing: a training-free block-sparse replacement for patch-patch global attention while keeping special-token interactions dense. This makes the method easy to retrofit into VGGT and pi3.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering pose and pointmap estimation across several common datasets, plus longer Tanks & Temples sequences. The special-token ablation and learned-projection ablation are useful.
The analysis of attention maps and layer skipping gives plausible evidence that mid-layer global attention is more selective and important, which helps motivate adaptive sparsification.
weaknesses: The core contribution is quite incremental. The method is largely an application/adaptation of existing block-sparse attention ideas, especially SpargeAttention, to VGGT/pi3. The paper does not convincingly establish a new algorithmic contribution beyond token partitioning and threshold choices.

The headline claims are overstated. The abstract claims up to 4x faster inference with comparable performance, but end-to-end speedups in Table 1 are often much smaller, and small inputs can even be slower. At high sparsity, accuracy drops sharply, e.g. Tanks & Temples RRA@5 for VGGT falls from 84.8 to 57.3 at 50 frames and from 73.4 to 46.0 on full sequences.

The technical description has a correctness issue: Eq. 2 uses elementwise multiplication by a binary mask before softmax, which does not implement sparse attention because masked logits become zero rather than excluded with -inf. This may be only a notation error, but it weakens confidence in the method presentation.

The speed evaluation is incomplete. The paper reports timings mainly on a single H100 setup and does not provide memory measurements, kernel overhead breakdowns, or comparisons to alternative acceleration baselines such as layer skipping, frame subsampling, local/window sparse patterns, native SpargeAttention variants, or different FlashAttention implementations.

The sparsity terminology is confusing and sometimes inconsistent. The text defines sparsity ratio as the ratio of computed entries to total entries, while figures/tables appear to treat sparsity as skipped or pruned attention. This makes the claimed trade-offs harder to interpret.

The evaluation does not sufficiently address robustness. There is little discussion of variance over frame sampling/order, scene type, failure cases, or sensitivity to block size/top-k/CDF hyperparameters beyond large tables. Since the method is heuristic and training-free, these robustness details matter.

The claim that the sparse attention corresponds to geometric matching is suggestive but not rigorously validated. The visualizations are interesting, but there is no quantitative comparison to ground-truth correspondences or analysis of when the selected blocks miss important matches.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives high-level implementation details and some training settings for an ablation, but key details such as exact kernels, block sizes in the main method, hardware/software versions, and code availability are not sufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in recent feed-forward multi-view reconstruction models: global attention becomes dominant as the number of views grows. The proposed block-sparse replacement is practical because it retrofits VGGT and pi3 without retraining the backbone.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering relative pose, pointmap estimation, and scene-level pose across many datasets, with full supplementary tables. Moderate sparsity settings consistently preserve much of the original performance while giving meaningful speedups on long sequences.

The analysis of attention structure is useful and well motivated. The paper connects sparse mid-layer patch-patch attention to cross-view correspondence behavior, and the layer-drop and special-token ablations support the design choices.

The method is simple and potentially useful: separating special-token interactions from sparse patch-patch attention is a clear implementation detail that materially improves robustness at high sparsity.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental. The method largely adapts known block-sparse attention and SpargeAttention-style mask selection to VGGT/pi3, so the main contribution is an effective application and analysis rather than a fundamentally new sparse-attention mechanism.

The headline claim of comparable performance up to large speedups is overstated. At high sparsity, especially the 75% setting used for the largest speedups, pose metrics can drop substantially; for example Tanks & Temples RRA@5 falls from about 84 to 57 for VGGT at 200 frames, and similar drops appear for pi3. The convincing regime is moderate sparsity, not the most aggressive setting.

Runtime evidence is narrower than the accuracy evaluation. Detailed timing is mainly reported on Tanks & Temples with an H100 and one resolution, with limited breakdown of mask construction overhead, memory savings, or portability across hardware and sequence/resolution regimes.

Reproducibility could be stronger. The paper gives many hyperparameter settings through Top-k/CDF tables, but the implementation details of the sparse kernel integration, exact block sizes for the main experiments, and code availability are not clearly specified in the manuscript.

The attention-pattern analysis is suggestive but not fully rigorous. Visual correspondences and average/max attention statistics support the motivation, but the paper does not quantitatively validate that selected sparse blocks correspond to true geometric matches or analyze failure modes when sparsity removes important interactions.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in recent feed-forward multi-view geometry transformers: global attention becomes dominant as the number of views grows. The motivation is well supported by runtime profiling and attention-map analysis.

The proposed method is practical and lightweight: a training-free block-sparse replacement for patch-patch global attention, while preserving dense interactions for camera/register tokens. This is a useful engineering contribution for scaling existing models without retraining.

Evaluation breadth is strong. The method is applied to VGGT, pi3, and MapAnything, and tested on pose and reconstruction benchmarks including Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D, and Tanks & Temples, with additional long-sequence ScanNet experiments up to 1000 frames.

The empirical trends are convincing: accuracy degrades gradually with sparsity and often remains close to the dense model at moderate sparsity, while random masking and simpler variants fail more quickly. The ablations on special-token handling, learned projections, layer dropping, and alternative sparse attention baselines support the design choices.
The paper is mostly clear and well organized, with intuitive visualizations connecting sparse attention patterns to cross-view geometric correspondences.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. The work largely adapts existing block-sparse attention ideas and kernels, especially SpargeAttention-style pooled query-key block selection, to multi-view geometry transformers. The main contribution is a strong application and empirical study rather than a fundamentally new sparse-attention mechanism.

The speedup evidence is less complete than the accuracy evidence. The paper claims more than 3x inference acceleration, but detailed wall-clock tables are not provided for most settings; some appendix text reports about 2x at 60% sparsity and up to 3x only for longer sequences. Measurements are mostly H100-specific and do not thoroughly separate mask construction overhead, kernel speed, memory savings, preprocessing/postprocessing, or batch/sequence-length effects.

The theoretical FLOP analysis appears underspecified and possibly inconsistent: the notation in the block FLOP formula uses T where t is expected, and the total FLOP expression seems to omit an explicit multiplier for the number of global attention blocks. This weakens the formal support for the reported theoretical speedups.

The mathematical description of sparse attention is imprecise: multiplying logits by a binary mask before softmax does not correctly remove masked entries unless masked positions are set to negative infinity or handled by the sparse kernel. The implementation may be correct, but the paper’s equation is technically misleading.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important implementation details such as default block sizes, exact kernel configuration, chosen operating points, hardware/software environment, and code availability are not sufficiently specified in the main text. The many rho/CDF settings make it hard to know which configuration a practitioner should use by default.

The evaluation mostly tests drop-in inference sparsification of already strong models, but does not deeply analyze failure cases, scenes with weak overlap or repeated structures, calibration/pose-quality sensitivity, memory limits, or behavior at higher image resolutions, despite claiming applicability to high-resolution inference.

Dense baseline values are often communicated through plots rather than full tables, making exact comparison and significance hard to assess. Some apparent improvements under sparsification are attributed to randomness, but variance over runs, permutations, or sampling choices is not systematically reported.

strengths: The paper targets a real bottleneck in modern feed-forward multi-view geometry transformers: global attention becomes dominant as the number of views grows. The motivation is credible and relevant to CVPR.

The proposed training-free block-sparse replacement is simple and practically attractive. Keeping special-token interactions dense while sparsifying patch-patch attention is a sensible design choice and is supported by ablations.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad: VGGT, pi3, and MapAnything are tested across pose estimation, pointmap/reconstruction benchmarks, and longer-sequence settings. The paper includes comparisons to random masks, SpargeAttention-style variants, special-token ablations, and learned projection variants.

Results generally support the main qualitative claim that substantial sparsity can be introduced with modest degradation, especially at moderate sparsity levels, and that long-sequence inference can be accelerated.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited. The method is largely an adaptation of existing block-sparse attention ideas, especially SpargeAttention-style pooled query-key mask prediction, to multi-view geometry transformers. The new contribution is mostly task-specific engineering rather than a fundamentally new sparse attention method.

The headline speedup claims are somewhat overstated relative to the evidence. The manuscript repeatedly emphasizes more than 3x acceleration, but the detailed results indicate smaller end-to-end gains in many realistic settings, with around 2x reported for several long-sequence cases and theoretical speedups separated from measured wall-clock results.

The runtime evaluation lacks important reproducibility details: exact kernel implementation, block sizes for the main experiments, precision, batching, warmup/timing protocol, memory behavior, and preprocessing/postprocessing accounting are not fully specified. This is material because the paper’s contribution is primarily efficiency.

The paper does not demonstrate that the sparse attention approximation is robust beyond the tested model family and task setup. The approach is evaluated only by modifying already strong pretrained systems, so the contribution depends heavily on those models’ existing behavior.

Accuracy degradation is non-negligible at higher sparsity on several datasets and models, even though the narrative sometimes frames performance as essentially preserved. The trade-off is useful, but the claims should be more carefully calibrated.

Some technical exposition is imprecise, for example the sparse attention equation uses elementwise multiplication by a binary mask before softmax, which would not be equivalent to masking with negative infinity unless handled differently in the kernel. This does not necessarily invalidate the implementation, but it weakens clarity.

The analysis of attention as geometric correspondence is plausible and visually appealing, but mostly qualitative. Stronger quantitative correspondence analysis would make the central motivation more convincing.

strengths: The paper targets a real bottleneck in recent multi-view geometry transformers: dense global attention becomes dominant as the number of views grows. The motivation is well supported by runtime measurements and attention-map analysis showing strong sparsity in patch-patch interactions.

The method is simple and practical: a training-free block-sparse replacement using pooled query-key similarities, top-k plus CDF thresholding, and dense treatment of special tokens. This makes it easy to retrofit into existing models without retraining.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this problem setting. Results cover VGGT, pi3, and MapAnything across relative pose, pointmap estimation, scene-level pose, and long-sequence settings, with datasets including RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D, and Tanks & Temples.

The paper includes useful ablations: random masking, SpargeAttention-style alternatives, special-token handling, learned mask projections, layer skipping, and long-sequence speed/accuracy behavior. These substantiate several key design choices.

The practical gains are meaningful. The reported speedups reach about 2x on 200-frame Tanks & Temples / longer ScanNet settings and up to around 3x on longer sequences, while maintaining comparable accuracy up to moderate or high sparsity.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. The work mainly adapts existing block-sparse attention ideas, especially SpargeAttention-style mask construction and kernels, to multi-view geometry transformers. The contribution is more application/analysis/engineering than a fundamentally new attention method.

The strongest runtime claims are not always as comprehensively reported as the accuracy claims. Main-text figures emphasize sparsity-performance tradeoffs, while detailed wall-clock measurements are mostly in the appendix and partly qualified, e.g. MapAnything timing is said to be inaccurate due to preprocessing/postprocessing.

The method depends on tunable sparsity/CDF thresholds, but the paper does not fully clarify how these should be selected for a new model, dataset, resolution, or accuracy budget. This leaves some reproducibility and deployment ambiguity despite the training-free framing.

The attention-sparsity interpretation as geometric correspondence search is plausible and visually compelling, but the evidence is mostly qualitative/statistical. There is limited direct validation that selected sparse blocks correspond to true geometric correspondences or that failures are explained by missing such correspondences.

Performance degradation at high sparsity can be nontrivial on some tasks/models, and the paper sometimes frames results as comparable to state of the art even when the more relevant comparison is loss relative to the original dense backbone. A clearer accuracy-speed Pareto summary would make the tradeoffs easier to assess.

Reproducibility would benefit from more implementation specifics: exact kernel version, hardware/software settings, memory measurements, threshold defaults per model, and whether code will be released. The method is understandable, but exact reproduction of the speedups may be difficult from the manuscript alone.
